warmup.q: You rebuild your service's JAR with a bug fix but keep the AOT cache from the previous build. You start it on JDK 25.0.4 with -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. What happens?
options: It runs the fixed code with the full speed-up from the cache
It runs the old code, served from the cache
It warns that the JAR changed, ignores the cache, and runs the fixed code with no archive at all
warmup.why: On 25.0.4 and later the JVM compares the JAR with the cache, prints a warning, and in the default auto mode carries on without the cache, and without the default CDS archive too. On 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 the check was missing and the old classes really did run (bug JDK-8377932). It only refuses to start if you asked for that with -XX:AOTMode=on.

sections.h: The JDK already ships a class archive
sections.html:
Start with the cost. Turn sharing off and java -version alone makes the JVM find, parse and verify 440 classes before it prints one line. On a shared 4-vCPU VM that doubled the Create VM time from lesson 1, from about 27 ms to about 54 ms, and lesson 1's tiny service needed about 250 ms instead of about 180 ms to its first 200.

Most JDK builds since JDK 12 avoid most of that work. They ship a class data sharing (CDS) archive, lib/server/classes.jsa, holding about 1,300 core JDK classes. The file does not contain class files. It contains the JVM's own internal structures for those classes, the ones it would otherwise build in metaspace, already parsed and verified, laid out as they sit in memory. At start-up the JVM memory-maps the file: it asks the OS to make the file part of its address space, so pages are read from disk only when they are touched. Then it fixes up the pointers and uses the classes as they are. This happens by default; -Xshare:off turns it off.

java -version shows it. On JDK 21 that command loads 405 classes, and all 405 say source: shared objects file. With -Xshare:off it loads 440 classes and none are shared. The extra 35 are classes the JVM has to generate at run time when there is no archive to take them from.

A JDK 21 package has two archives: classes.jsa (14.6 MB here) and classes_nocoops.jsa, for when compressed object pointers (32-bit object references, the default for heaps under 32 GB) are off. JDK 25 adds two _coh variants for compact object headers, a smaller object header layout that JEP 519 made a product feature in JDK 25 (still off by default). The JVM picks the archive that matches its flags.

That tells you what CDS can and can't save. It saves the find, parse and verify steps from lesson 1. It does not run static initializers: those still run on first use, in the same order, so a class whose <clinit> takes 400 ms takes 400 ms with any archive. A test program that logs its initializer order printed identical output with and without a JDK 21 archive and a JDK 25 AOT cache. It also does nothing for the JIT, which still starts cold.

Old articles also sell CDS as a way for JVMs on one host to share memory. Count on start-up time instead. Since JDK 21 the JVM maps archives at an alternative address by default (the log says ArchiveRelocationMode == 1), and patching the pointers writes to most pages, which makes them private. In one JDK 25 process, 11.5 MiB of the 14.4 MiB resident in the AOT cache's mapping were private dirty pages.

sections.h: AppCDS puts your own classes in the archive
sections.html:
The default archive covers the JDK. AppCDS adds your own classes. It has been part of OpenJDK since JDK 10, and on JDK 21 it is the start-up gain you can have today without touching code. There are three ways to build one.

The dynamic archive (JDK 13 and later) needs one training run. The JVM writes the archive when that run exits:

java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main   # training run
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main      # every start after

It stores only what the default archive lacks, so it is small: 1.47 MB for a 300-class app, where the static archive below was 12.9 MB because it holds the JDK classes too.

The static archive takes three steps: record the class list, dump it, use it.

java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main
java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main

-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive (JDK 19 and later), used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, folds this into your normal start command. If the file exists and came from the same JDK, the JVM uses it; if not, it writes one at exit. That is handy on a laptop and wrong for an immutable container: the file disappears with the pod, or the filesystem is read-only. Build the archive when you build the image.

On JDK 21, on a shared 4-vCPU VM, the 300-class app's median CPU time fell from 349 ms with the default archive to 171 ms with a dynamic archive and 178 ms with a static one. Wall time fell from 333 ms to 196 ms and 191 ms. Your absolute numbers will differ. The halving is what carries over.

The archive has rules. The class path must be JAR files, not directories of classes. The class path at run time must be the same as when the archive was made, or start with it. If a JAR changed after the archive was made, the JVM refuses the archive with warnings such as h21.jar timestamp has changed and size has changed, and runs normally from the JARs. It keeps using the default archive for the JDK classes. On JDK 21 this check works; keep that in mind for the last section.

Check: in development you run the app with -cp build/classes/java/main:libs/*.jar and add -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa. What happens at exit? (JDK 21 refuses: Cannot have non-empty directory in paths. Package the classes into a JAR first, as the Try it does.)

try.title: Climb the archive ladder
steps: Read ArchiveLadder. It packs its own package into startup/build/boot02/app.jar (CDS wants JARs), then runs the same small workload under each setup and counts the source: lines.
Predict the "from archive" column for the dynamic AppCDS row, then run it.
Run the Kotlin twin. Its class path is the app JAR plus kotlin-stdlib, and both go into the archive.

Gradle runs demos on the JDK that runs Gradle. If that is JDK 21, run the class with a JDK 25 java to get the AOT cache row: java -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder.

code.title: ArchiveLadder.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l02.demo; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.function.Predicate; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Packs this demo package into build/boot02/app.jar, then starts it under each class-sharing * setup: no sharing, the default CDS archive, a dynamic AppCDS archive, and on JDK 25+ the * AOT cache. For each it prints classes loaded, classes from an archive, and the median wall * time of 3 runs. Timings are noisy; the class counts are the part to trust. */ public class ArchiveLadder { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { Work.run(); return; } Path classes = Path.of(ArchiveLadder.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("boot02"); // startup/build/boot02 Files.createDirectories(dir); Path jar = packJar(classes, dir.resolve("app.jar")); // CDS wants JARs, not directories List<String> app = List.of("-cp", jar.toString(), ArchiveLadder.class.getName(), "--work"); System.out.printf("JDK %s, app %s%n", Runtime.version(), jar); System.out.printf("%-20s %8s %13s %10s%n", "setup", "loaded", "from archive", "wall ms"); row("no sharing", List.of("-Xshare:off"), app); row("default CDS", List.of(), app); Path jsa = dir.resolve("app.jsa"); // 1. training run: archive written at exit Files.deleteIfExists(jsa); run(List.of("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + jsa), app); row("AppCDS (dynamic)", List.of("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + jsa), app); if (Runtime.version().feature() >= 25) { Path aot = dir.resolve("app.aot"); // 2. JEP 514: train and assemble in one command Files.deleteIfExists(aot); run(List.of("-XX:AOTCacheOutput=" + aot), app); row("AOT cache", List.of("-XX:AOTCache=" + aot), app); System.out.printf("archive sizes: app.jsa %,d bytes, app.aot %,d bytes%n", Files.size(jsa), Files.size(aot)); } else { System.out.printf("archive size: app.jsa %,d bytes. Run on JDK 25+ to add the AOT cache row.%n", Files.size(jsa)); } } /** One line of the table: one logged run for the class counts, three quiet runs for the time. */ static void row(String name, List<String> flags, List<String> app) throws Exception { List<String> logged = new ArrayList<>(flags); logged.add("-Xlog:class+load"); List<String> lines = run(logged, app); long loaded = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")).count(); long shared = lines.stream().filter(l -> l.endsWith("source: shared objects file")).count(); long[] ms = new long[3]; for (int i = 0; i < ms.length; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); run(flags, app); ms[i] = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } java.util.Arrays.sort(ms); System.out.printf("%-20s %8d %13d %10d%n", name, loaded, shared, ms[1]); } /** Runs a child JVM with these flags and returns its output lines. */ static List<String> run(List<String> flags, List<String> app) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(app); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> out = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); if (p.waitFor() != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("child failed: " + cmd + "\n" + String.join("\n", out)); return out; } /** Puts every class file of this package into a JAR. */ static Path packJar(Path classes, Path jar) throws IOException { Path pkg = classes.resolve("workbench/startup/l02/demo"); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(file); Stream<Path> files = Files.list(pkg)) { for (Path f : files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".class")).sorted().toList()) { out.putNextEntry(new JarEntry(classes.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'))); out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)); out.closeEntry(); } } return jar; } /** The "service" being started: a few classes, lambdas, a stream, regex, java.time and formatting. */ static final class Work { record Payment(String id, long amountMinor, String currency) { } enum Status { AUTHORIZED, DECLINED } static void run() { Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+);(\\d+);([A-Z]{3})"); List<Payment> payments = Stream.of("p1;1250;EUR", "p2;990;EUR", "p3;150000;USD", "p4;20;GBP") .map(line::matcher) .filter(m -> m.matches()) .map(m -> new Payment(m.group(1), Long.parseLong(m.group(2)), m.group(3))) .toList(); Predicate<Payment> withinLimit = p -> p.amountMinor() <= 100_000; Map<Status, List<String>> byStatus = payments.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy( p -> withinLimit.test(p) ? Status.AUTHORIZED : Status.DECLINED, TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Payment::id, Collectors.toList()))); String report = String.format("%s %s", LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2), byStatus); if (report.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } } }

For each it prints classes loaded, classes from an archive, and the * median wall time of 3 runs. Timings are noisy; the class counts are the part to trust. */ private object Anchor private data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String) private enum class Status { AUTHORIZED, DECLINED } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val classes = Path.of(Anchor::class.java.protectionDomain.codeSource.location.toURI()) val dir = classes.parent.parent.parent.resolve("boot02") // startup/build/boot02 Files.createDirectories(dir) val jar = packJar(classes, dir.resolve("app-kt.jar")) // CDS wants JARs, not directories val stdlib = Path.of(KotlinVersion::class.java.protectionDomain.codeSource.location.toURI()) val classPath = listOf(jar, stdlib).joinToString(java.io.File.pathSeparator) val app = listOf("-cp", classPath, "workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadderKt", "--work") println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, app $jar (+ kotlin-stdlib)") println("%-20s %8s %13s %10s".format("setup", "loaded", "from archive", "wall ms")) row("no sharing", listOf("-Xshare:off"), app) row("default CDS", emptyList(), app) val jsa = dir.resolve("app-kt.jsa") // 1. training run: archive written at exit jsa.deleteIfExists() run(listOf("-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=$jsa"), app) row("AppCDS (dynamic)", listOf("-XX:SharedArchiveFile=$jsa"), app) if (Runtime.version().feature() >= 25) { val aot = dir.resolve("app-kt.aot") // 2. JEP 514: train and assemble in one command aot.deleteIfExists() run(listOf("-XX:AOTCacheOutput=$aot"), app) row("AOT cache", listOf("-XX:AOTCache=$aot"), app) println("archive sizes: app-kt.jsa %,d bytes, app-kt.aot %,d bytes".format(jsa.fileSize(), aot.fileSize())) } else { println("archive size: app-kt.jsa %,d bytes. Run on JDK 25+ to add the AOT cache row.".format(jsa.fileSize())) } } /** One line of the table: one logged run for the class counts, three quiet runs for the time. */ private fun row(name: String, flags: List<String>, app: List<String>) { val lines = run(flags + "-Xlog:class+load", app) val loaded = lines.count { " source: " in it } val shared = lines.count { it.endsWith("source: shared objects file") } val ms = List(3) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() run(flags, app) (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 }.sorted() println("%-20s %8d %13d %10d".format(name, loaded, shared, ms[1])) } /** Runs a child JVM with these flags and returns its output lines. */ private fun run(flags: List<String>, app: List<String>): List<String> { val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + flags + app val p = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val out = p.inputReader().readLines() check(p.waitFor() == 0) { "child failed: $cmd\n${out.joinToString("\n")}" } return out } /** Puts every class file of this package into a JAR. */ private fun packJar(classes: Path, jar: Path): Path { JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar)).use { out -> for (f in classes.resolve("workbench/startup/l02/demo").listDirectoryEntries("*.class").sorted()) { out.putNextEntry(JarEntry(classes.relativize(f).toString().replace('\\', '/'))) out.write(Files.readAllBytes(f)) out.closeEntry() } } return jar } /** The "service" being started: a few classes, lambdas, regex, java.time and formatting. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+);(\d+);([A-Z]{3})""") val payments = listOf("p1;1250;EUR", "p2;990;EUR", "p3;150000;USD", "p4;20;GBP") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .map { (id, amount, currency) -> Payment(id, amount.toLong(), currency) } val withinLimit: (Payment) -> Boolean = { it.amountMinor <= 100_000 } val byStatus = payments .groupBy({ if (withinLimit(it)) Status.AUTHORIZED else Status.DECLINED }, { it.id }) .toSortedMap() val report = "%s %s".format(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 2), byStatus) check(report.isNotEmpty()) }

sections.h: Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, run
sections.html:
Project Leyden is the OpenJDK project that moves start-up work out of production runs. Its first result is the AOT cache, built one JEP at a time:

JDK What arrived
24 JEP 483: the AOT cache, with classes already loaded and linked; flags -XX:AOTMode, -XX:AOTConfiguration, -XX:AOTCache
25 (LTS) JEP 514: one-step -XX:AOTCacheOutput. JEP 515: method profiles from training, for faster warm-up
26 JEP 516: the full cache works with every GC, ZGC included
27 no Leyden JEP; -XX:AOTMode=required becomes the name for on
28, in development JEP 544: compiled code in the cache

The java man page names three phases. In training you run the app with a representative workload, and the JVM records what it loaded and linked into an AOT configuration file. In assembly the JVM turns that file into the cache; your application does not run. In production you start with the cache. On JDK 25 one command does the first two:

java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main   # training + assembly, JDK 25+
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main         # production

When training and assembly run in different pipeline stages, use the two-step form from JDK 24:

java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main
java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar

The one-step command does the same underneath: after training it starts a second JVM with -XX:AOTMode=create, passing the settings through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

The cache holds more than an AppCDS archive. Normally the JVM resolves references lazily: the first time an instruction runs, it turns a symbolic name in the constant pool, such as java/util/Map.get, into a pointer to the real method. The first run of a lambda does more: its invokedynamic instruction calls a bootstrap method that generates the lambda's hidden class. The AOT cache stores the results of that work from the training run: classes already linked, those references and invokedynamic call sites already resolved (these modes switch on -XX:+AOTClassLinking), Java objects the JVM would build at start-up, such as its module graph, and on JDK 25 the method profiles, the counts that tell the JIT what is hot. The JVM loads and links every cached class before main runs, so it reports more classes loaded than without the cache, all from the archive. Code that training never ran gets none of this; it is resolved lazily, as before.

On JDK 25 on the same VM, the 300-class app went from 504 ms of CPU to 81 ms, from 431 ms to 98 ms of wall time, and from 64 MiB to 42 MiB of max RSS. A JDK HttpServer app's median time to first request fell from 218 ms to 136 ms. Quarkus's perf lab measured time to first request of 4,417 ms in JVM mode and 1,859 ms with the cache, with peak throughput about 7% lower.

Quarkus 3.40 wires it up for you. Set quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true and it trains the cache while your @QuarkusIntegrationTests run and writes target/quarkus-app/app.aot; start with java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar quarkus-run.jar. Its aot-jar packaging leaves all class loading to the JDK's own loaders, because Leyden does not support custom class loaders yet. The docs add the rule the lab makes concrete: "The more representative your integration tests are of production traffic, the more effective the AOT cache will be."

sections.h: A cache is valid for one JAR, one JDK and one set of flags
sections.html:
The man page is blunt: a cache belongs to one application class path, one JDK release, and one OS and CPU, and "if any of the above changes, you must recreate the AOT cache". The JVM checks, and in the default auto mode it starts without the cache when a check fails.

A changed JAR is the worst case, because on early JDK 25 builds the check was missing. On 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 and on 26.0.0 to 26.0.1, the JVM never compared the application's JARs with the cache (bug JDK-8377932). Rebuild the JAR, keep the old app.aot, and the JVM serves the old classes. This is JDK 25 GA running a JAR rebuilt to print "version TWO":

[info][class,load] stale.Hello source: shared objects file
version ONE

The fix shipped in JDK 27 and was backported to 25.0.4 and 26.0.2. The same run on 25.0.4.1 rejects the cache and runs the new code:

[warning][aot] This file is not the one used while building the AOT cache: 'hello.jar', timestamp has changed, size has changed
[error  ][aot] shared class paths mismatch (hint: enable -Xlog:class+path=info to diagnose the failure)
version TWO, rebuilt

So require JDK 25.0.4 or later (26.0.2 or later on 26), and rebuild the cache with every JAR, in the same build step, shipped in the same image layer. On a fixed JDK an old cache can't run old code, but it still costs you the whole speed-up.

An AOT cache the JVM can't use leaves you with no archive at all. It does not fall back to the default CDS archive. A one-class program loaded 542 classes from the default archive with no flag, and 0 with a stale or missing cache file. A typo in the path makes start-up slower than no flag.

A different GC breaks it on JDK 25. A cache trained under G1 gave 0 archived classes under -XX:+UseZGC. Training under ZGC worked only partly: CPU fell from 610 ms to 439 ms, against 504 ms to 81 ms with G1. JDK 26's JEP 516 removes this limit. Until then, train with the GC you run.

Module and agent options must match too. --module-path, --add-modules and --enable-native-access should be the same in training and production. Quarkus documents one trap: -XX:StartFlightRecording quietly adds the jdk.jfr module, and the cache no longer matches. The man page also lists "certain JVMTI options" as incompatible. JVMTI is the JVM's tool interface, the one monitoring (APM) agents use to rewrite classes as they load, so this matters as soon as someone attaches an agent.

Two flags catch all of this. -Xlog:aot prints Opened AOT cache app.aot. when the cache works and the reason when it doesn't. -XX:AOTMode=on (JDK 24 to 26; required from JDK 27) makes the JVM exit instead of running without the cache. Use that in CI. Keep it out of production: the JDK 27 man page warns that your application "may fail to launch" if something like a cloud provider's monitoring agent adds an incompatible option.

Check with the mechanism: you train on JDK 25.0.4 with G1, then deploy the same JAR on 25.0.5 with G1. Does the cache load? (No. The cache records the exact JDK build, and the JVM refuses one made by a different build.)

try.title: Run new code with an old cache
steps: Read StaleCacheDemo. It compiles a one-class program that prints "version ONE", trains a cache on it, rebuilds the JAR to print "version TWO", and starts the new JAR with the old cache.
Run it through Gradle. On JDK 21 it uses a dynamic CDS archive, because there is no AOT cache.

If you have a JDK 25, run it with that JDK's java directly: java -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l02.demo.StaleCacheDemo. Check java -version first and predict which output you'll get.

code.title: StaleCacheDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.startup.l02.demo; import javax.tools.JavaCompiler; import javax.tools.ToolProvider; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.jar.JarEntry; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; /** * Builds hello.jar printing "version ONE", trains a cache on it, rebuilds the JAR to print * "version TWO", and runs the new JAR with the old cache. On JDK 25+ the cache is an AOT cache; * on older JDKs it is a dynamic CDS archive. Needs a JDK (it compiles Java source). */ public class StaleCacheDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path classes = Path.of(StaleCacheDemo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource().getLocation().toURI()); Path dir = classes.getParent().getParent().getParent().resolve("boot02-stale"); Files.createDirectories(dir); Path jar = dir.resolve("hello.jar"); boolean aot = Runtime.version().feature() >= 25; Path cache = dir.resolve(aot ? "hello.aot" : "hello.jsa"); Files.deleteIfExists(cache); // 1. build version ONE and train a cache on it build(dir, jar, "version ONE"); run(List.of(aot ? "-XX:AOTCacheOutput=" + cache : "-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=" + cache), jar); // 2. rebuild the JAR, as a new commit would, but keep the old cache build(dir, jar, "version TWO, rebuilt"); // 3. production: new JAR, old cache String flag = aot ? "-XX:AOTCache=" + cache : "-XX:SharedArchiveFile=" + cache; System.out.printf("JDK %s: java %s -cp hello.jar stale.Hello%n", Runtime.version(), flag.replace(dir + "/", "")); for (String line : run(List.of(flag, "-Xlog:class+load"), jar)) { if (line.contains("stale.Hello source:") || line.startsWith("version") || line.contains("[warning]") || line.contains("[error")) { System.out.println(" " + line.replace("file:" + dir + "/", "file:").replace(dir + "/", "")); } } } /** Compiles a one-class program that prints {@code message} and packs it into {@code jar}. */ static void build(Path dir, Path jar, String message) throws Exception { Path src = dir.resolve("src/stale/Hello.java"); Files.createDirectories(src.getParent()); Files.writeString(src, "package stale;\npublic class Hello {\n public static void main(String[] a) {\n" + " System.out.println(\"" + message + "\");\n }\n}\n"); Path out = dir.resolve("classes"); JavaCompiler javac = ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler(); if (javac == null) throw new IllegalStateException("run this on a JDK, not a JRE"); if (javac.run(null, null, null, "-d", out.toString(), src.toString()) != 0) throw new IllegalStateException("javac failed"); Files.deleteIfExists(jar); try (OutputStream file = Files.newOutputStream(jar); JarOutputStream j = new JarOutputStream(file)) { j.putNextEntry(new JarEntry("stale/Hello.class")); j.write(Files.readAllBytes(out.resolve("stale/Hello.class"))); j.closeEntry(); } } static List<String> run(List<String> flags, Path jar) throws Exception { List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(flags); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", jar.toString(), "stale.Hello")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); List<String> out = p.inputReader().lines().toList(); p.waitFor(); return out; } }

try.expect: JDK 21 refuses the archive (hello.jar size has changed, Unable to use shared archive) and prints version TWO, rebuilt. JDK 25 GA (25+36) prints stale.Hello source: shared objects file and version ONE: the old class, from the cache. JDK 25.0.4 and later print the timestamp has changed, size has changed warning, Unable to map shared spaces, and version TWO, rebuilt, loaded from the JAR.

refs.title: The fix: 8377932, AOT cache is not rejected when JAR file has changed

analogy: Without CDS, the JVM is a librarian who unpacks every book each morning, reads it, checks it for errors and only then shelves it. CDS is a bookcase that arrives already filled: you wheel it in and open the doors. The AOT cache is the same bookcase with the cross-references between books already filled in and sticky notes on the pages people read most. A training run is the day you watch which books people actually take. The analogy breaks at the worst place: a librarian would notice that the books in the wheeled-in bookcase are last year's edition. JDK 25 before 25.0.4 didn't.
world: For a Quarkus 3.40 payment service on JDK 25, the cheapest start-up win is one property: quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true, with the cache trained by your @QuarkusIntegrationTests. Make those tests look like production: if they only authorize cards, the refund and chargeback code paths load the slow way in every new pod. Pin the JDK patch level in your base image to 25.0.4 or later, train in the same image you run, and copy app.aot in the same layer as the JAR. Run a CI step with -XX:AOTMode=on -Xlog:aot that fails the build if the cache does not open, and leave AOTMode unset in production so an APM agent can't keep pods from starting. Services still on JDK 21 can use Quarkus's AppCDS fallback, quarkus.package.jar.aot.type=app-cds.
mistake: The costly mistake is treating the cache as a build artifact you make once and reuse. A pipeline caches app.aot to save a minute, the JAR changes, and on JDK 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 the service runs last week's classes with no error at all. On 25.0.4 and later it runs the right code, but with no archive, so every pod starts slower than before you added the cache, and only a warning line says why. The fix is to generate the cache in the same build step as the JAR, ship both together, require 25.0.4 or later, and let CI fail when -XX:AOTMode=on can't open it.

compare.title: A training entry point in Java and Kotlin

java.title: TrainingMain.java
java.html: /** Starts the service, drives every kind of request production sees, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ public final class TrainingMain { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { PaymentService service = PaymentService.start(); // the same wiring as production for (String fixture : List.of("authorize-eur.json", "authorize-usd.json", "refund.json", "capture.json")) { service.handle(Fixtures.load(fixture)); // real code paths, fake card issuer } service.stop(); System.exit(0); // JDK 24/25 write the training data when the JVM exits } }

kotlin.title: TrainingMain.kt
kotlin.html: /** Starts the service, drives every kind of request production sees, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ fun main() { val service = PaymentService.start() // the same wiring as production listOf("authorize-eur.json", "authorize-usd.json", "refund.json", "capture.json") .forEach { service.handle(Fixtures.load(it)) } // real code paths, fake card issuer service.stop() exitProcess(0) // JDK 24/25 write the training data when the JVM exits }

compare.note: The cache does not care which language produced the bytecode. What differs is the class path and the entry point. A Kotlin service has kotlin-stdlib (and often kotlinx-coroutines) as JARs on the class path, and they must be there in the same order in training and in production, or the cache is refused. The training entry point is TrainingMainKt, not TrainingMain. Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas to invokedynamic, like Java, so the cache can pre-resolve those call sites in both. Before JDK 26 the training run has to exit to write its data, which is why both versions end the process; JDK 26 adds jcmd <pid> AOT.end_recording for long-running servers.

worked.title: Add the AOT cache to a container build

steps.say: Pin the JDK and use the same image to build and to run. The cache records the exact JDK build: a cache made on 25 GA was refused on 25.0.4.1 with The AOT cache was created by a different version or build of HotSpot. Pick 25.0.4 or later, so a changed JAR can never run stale classes.
steps.code: # check the build stage and the runtime stage print the same line java -version 2>&1 | head -1 # openjdk version "25.0.4.1" ... must be 25.0.4 or later

steps.say: In the build stage, put the JAR at the path it will have at run time, then train and assemble in one step. Use the training entry point from the compare block, so the run exercises every request type and then exits.
steps.code: cp build/libs/pay.jar /srv/pay.jar java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/pay.jar com.acme.pay.TrainingMain # ... AOTCache creation is complete: /srv/app.aot ... bytes

steps.say: In CI, start the real entry point with -XX:AOTMode=on and -Xlog:aot and fail the build if the cache doesn't open. A wrong path, a different JDK or a changed JAR all make this exit with an error.
steps.code: java -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -Xlog:aot -cp /srv/pay.jar com.acme.pay.SmokeMain \ | grep -q 'Opened AOT cache' || { echo 'AOT cache not used'; exit 1; } # JDK 27+: AOTMode=required

steps.say: Ship pay.jar and app.aot in the same image layer and start production without AOTMode. If someone later attaches an agent that the cache can't handle, the pod starts slower instead of not at all.
steps.code: java -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot -cp /srv/pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main

lab.title: Write a recording class loader and a training run
steps: Run the tests once. All ten fail with NotImplementedError.

Implement RecordingClassLoader.loadClass. Outside the prefix, call super.loadClass(name, resolve). Inside it, take getClassLoadingLock(name), return findLoadedClass(name) if it is already there, otherwise read the class file from parent.getResourceAsStream, call defineClass, and record the name.

Implement defined() and run RecordingClassLoaderTest. Look at the first two tests: Class.forName(name, false, loader) defines one class, true defines two, because only initialization runs FeeTable's static initializer.
Implement TrainingRun.classList (a fresh loader, Class.forName(entryClass, true, loader), getMethod("handle", String::class.java), one invoke per request) and missing (one line of set arithmetic).
Run all tests until the ten pass. Read the fixtures in src/test/java/workbench/startup/l02/fixtures/: training with authorizations only never loads Refund.
hints: Kotlin's synchronized(lock) { ... } is inline, so return c inside it returns from loadClass.
parent.getResourceAsStream(path)?.use { it.readBytes() } ?: throw ClassNotFoundException(name) reads the bytes and handles a missing file in one expression.
The tests compare sets of class names, never counts. A count of all loaded classes changes between JDK builds; the classes your own loader defined do not.
lab.done: All ten tests in RecordingClassLoaderTest and TrainingRunTest pass.

drill.title: The commands from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. For pay.jar with main class com.acme.pay.Main, write: (1) the two JDK 21 commands for a dynamic AppCDS archive, (2) the two JDK 25 commands for an AOT cache, (3) the CI command that fails if the cache can't be used. Then add one comment saying which JDK patch level you require and why.

answer.html: # 1. JDK 21: dynamic AppCDS java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main # 2. JDK 25: AOT cache (training + assembly, then production) java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main # 3. CI only: exit with an error if the cache can't be used (AOTMode=required on JDK 27+) java -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -Xlog:aot -cp pay.jar com.acme.pay.Main # Require 25.0.4+ (or 26.0.2+): earlier builds don't check the JAR (JDK-8377932) # and can run stale classes. Rebuild app.aot with every pay.jar.

recap: CDS maps pre-parsed classes from a .jsa file. The default archive (JDK 12+) covers about 1,300 JDK classes; -Xshare:off turns it off.

AppCDS adds your classes: dynamic with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit and -XX:SharedArchiveFile, static with a class list and -Xshare:dump, or -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive. On JDK 21 it halved a test app's start-up CPU.
The AOT cache (JEP 483 in JDK 24, one-step -XX:AOTCacheOutput in JDK 25) adds linked classes and profiles. Training, assembly, production; a training run only captures the code paths it ran.
Require JDK 25.0.4+ or 26.0.2+ for the AOT cache, and rebuild it with every JAR: earlier builds could run stale classes (JDK-8377932).
An AOT cache the JVM can't use leaves no archive at all, not even the default one. Check with -Xlog:aot and -XX:AOTMode=on in CI, never in production.
Match the GC (ZGC needs JDK 26 for the full cache), the module flags and the class path between training and production.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to keep app.aot in the CI cache between builds, because training adds two minutes. Explain why that is a bad idea, and what happens on JDK 25.0.3 versus 25.0.4 when the JAR has changed.
explain.answer: The cache belongs to one exact set of JARs, one JDK build and one set of flags. When the JAR changes, the old cache describes classes that no longer exist in that form. On 25.0.3 the JVM didn't check the application JARs at all, so it would serve the old classes from the cache and run last build's code with no error. On 25.0.4 and later it notices the changed timestamp and size, warns, and runs without the cache, so the code is right but every pod loses the speed-up, and the default CDS archive too. Either way the cache has to be built in the same step as the JAR and shipped with it. The two minutes are cheaper than either failure.

deeper.html:
A few details that matter once you run this for real.

The static archive is dumped in interpreter-only mode, as if -Xint were set, so the output is deterministic, bit for bit. For big class lists you can add -Xmixed to speed up the dump when you don't need that.

You can also take an archive from a running process: jcmd <pid> VM.cds dynamic_dump app.jsa, if the process was started with -XX:+RecordDynamicDumpInfo, or jcmd <pid> VM.cds static_dump app.jsa. That suits a service whose real warm-up needs real traffic. To try flags without editing start scripts, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa works, because the JVM reads that variable at start.

In the AOT cache file names, %p and %t are replaced by the PID and the start time, as in -XX:AOTCacheOutput=pay%p.aot, so parallel training runs don't overwrite each other.

The man page lags behind the code in one place: the JDK 25 page still says the cache holds "Java classes and heap objects" and that profiles will come in a future release, although JEP 515 shipped profiles in JDK 25. The JDK 28 development page lists classes, heap objects, execution profiles and compiled methods.

What's next in Leyden, as of the JDK 28 development line: JEP 544 moves JIT compilation into the training run and ships the native code in the cache, while the JIT can still recompile in production. JEP 545 targets start-up and warm-up with ZGC. Neither is in a released JDK yet, so treat them as previews of where this is going, not as flags to use.
